questions.prompt: What is the transfer function \(H(s)\) of an LTI system?
options: The output when the input is a unit step
The ratio \(Y(s)/X(s)\) of the Laplace transforms of output and input with zero initial conditions, which equals the Laplace transform of the impulse response
The ratio \(X(s)/Y(s)\) of input to output
questions.explanation:
Transforming a linear ODE with zero initial conditions turns derivatives into powers of s, so the output transform is \(H(s)\) times the input transform, and \(H(s)=Y(s)/X(s)\). An impulse has transform 1, so \(H(s)\) is also the transform of \(h(t)\).
• A product would not be a property of the system alone.
• The step response is \(H(s)/s\), not \(H(s)\).
• \(X/Y\) is the inverse system.

questions.prompt: A system obeys \(3\ddot y+2\dot y+5y=4x\). With zero initial conditions, what is \(H(s)=Y(s)/X(s)\)?
questions.explanation:
Each derivative becomes a factor of s: \((3s^2+2s+5)Y(s)=4X(s)\), so \(H=4/(3s^2+2s+5)\).
• The flipped fraction is \(X/Y\).
• An extra s in the numerator would need a \(\dot x\) term on the right side.
• Reversing the coefficient order puts the 5 on \(s^2\); the highest derivative goes with the highest power.

questions.prompt: What is the DC (zero-frequency) gain of \(H(s)=\dfrac{2s+6}{s^2+4s+3}\)?
questions.explanation:
DC means \(s=0\): \(H(0)=6/3=2\). A constant input of 1 settles to an output of 2.
• Taking the ratio of the leading coefficients (\(2/1\) on \(s/s^2\)) describes high frequency, not DC; it gives a gain falling as \(2/s\).
• Answering 3 or 0.5 swaps or mixes the constant terms.

questions.prompt: A tank's level \(h\) (in m) responds to an inflow rate \(q\) (in \(\mathrm{m^3/s}\)). What are the units of the transfer function \(H(s)=h(s)/q(s)\) evaluated at a frequency?
options: \(\mathrm{s/m^2}\): output units divided by input units
Dimensionless, because transfer functions are always ratios of like quantities
questions.explanation:
A transfer function carries output units over input units: \(\mathrm{m}/(\mathrm{m^3/s})=\mathrm{s/m^2}\). Gains between unlike quantities (force to position, flow to level, voltage to speed) are normal in system models.
• \(\mathrm{m^2/s}\) is the inverse.
• Dimensionless gains only occur when input and output share units.
• \(\mathrm{m^4/s}\) multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: A system has transfer function \(G(j\omega_{0})=0.8\angle-30^{\circ}\) at the operating frequency \(\omega_{0}\). The input is \(x(t)=5\cos(\omega_{0}t+20^{\circ})\). What is the output at \(t=0\)?
questions.explanation:
Output amplitude \(=5\times 0.8=4\). Output phase \(=\) input phase \(+\angle G=20^{\circ}+(-30^{\circ})=-10^{\circ}\).
So \(y(t)=4\cos(\omega_{0}t-10^{\circ})\) and \(y(0)=4\cos(-10^{\circ})=4\times 0.9848=3.939\).
Common mistake: using only the transfer function's phase \((4\cos(-30^{\circ})=3.46)\) and forgetting the input's own +20° phase.

questions.prompt: Two LTI blocks are connected in series: \(H_1(s)=\dfrac{2}{s+1}\) followed by \(H_2(s)=\dfrac{5}{s+10}\). What is the magnitude of the overall frequency response at \(\omega=1\ \mathrm{rad/s}\)?
questions.explanation:
Series blocks multiply: \(H=H_1H_2\), so \(|H|=|H_1||H_2|\). At \(\omega=1\): \(|H_1|=2/\sqrt2=1.414\) and \(|H_2|=5/\sqrt{101}=0.498\), so \(|H|=0.704\).
• Adding the magnitudes (1.91) treats a series connection as parallel.
• Using DC gains gives \(2\times0.5=1\).

questions.prompt: Two blocks are connected in parallel, with their outputs added: \(H_1=\dfrac{1}{s+2}\) and \(H_2=\dfrac{3}{s+4}\). The combined transfer function has one zero. What is its magnitude (distance from the origin)?
questions.explanation:
\(H=\dfrac{1}{s+2}+\dfrac{3}{s+4}=\dfrac{(s+4)+3(s+2)}{(s+2)(s+4)}=\dfrac{4s+10}{(s+2)(s+4)}\). The zero is at \(s=-2.5\). Parallel paths can create zeros that neither block has alone.
• Multiplying the blocks instead gives \(3/((s+2)(s+4))\), which has no finite zero.
• Answering 2 or 4 picks a pole, not the zero.

questions.prompt: A block \(G(s)=\dfrac{K}{s+a}\) is placed in a unity negative-feedback loop. What is the closed-loop transfer function?
questions.explanation:
\(\dfrac{G}{1+G}=\dfrac{K/(s+a)}{1+K/(s+a)}=\dfrac{K}{s+a+K}\). The pole moves from \(-a\) to \(-(a+K)\): feedback speeds up the response.
• A minus sign belongs to positive feedback.
• The open-loop G ignores the loop.
• \((s+a)/(s+a+K)\) is the error response \(1/(1+G)\), not the output.

questions.prompt: A system has transfer function \(H=0.5\angle-90^{\circ}\) at the frequency of the input \(x(t)=2\sin(\omega t)\). Which is the steady-state output?
questions.explanation:
The amplitude is \(2\times 0.5=1\), and the phase shift is −90° applied to a sine: \(1\cdot\sin(\omega t-90^{\circ})\). Since \(\sin(x-90^{\circ})=-\cos(x)\), the output is \(-\cos(\omega t)\).
• \(\sin(\omega t)\) ignores the phase shift.
• \(\cos(\omega t)\) has the wrong sign: \(\sin(x-90^{\circ})=-\cos x\), not \(+\cos x\). (\(\sin(x+90^{\circ})\) would give \(+\cos x\).)
• \(-\sin(\omega t)\) is a 180° shift, not 90°.

questions.prompt: Preview of poles and zeros. \(H(s)=\dfrac{s+4}{s^2+5s+6}\). The poles are the roots of the denominator. What is the magnitude of the pole farthest from the origin?
questions.explanation:
\(s^2+5s+6=(s+2)(s+3)\), so the poles are at \(-2\) and \(-3\); the farthest is at distance 3. The numerator root \(-4\) is a zero, not a pole.
• Answering 4 picks the zero.
• Answering 6 reads the constant term, which is the product of the pole magnitudes.

questions.prompt: Preview of feedback. A later skill shows that when a forward block with gain A is wrapped in a feedback path with gain \(\beta\), the overall (closed-loop) transfer function is \(A/(1+A\beta)\). Find the closed-loop gain for A \(=1000\) and \(\beta=0.1\).
questions.explanation:
\(A_{\mathrm{cl}}=1000/(1+1000\times 0.1)=1000/101=9.901\), very close to \(1/\beta=10\).
Each block is a transfer function, and the loop combines them algebraically. Common mistake: computing \(A/(1+A)\ (=0.999\), forgetting \(\beta\)) or \(1/(1+A\beta)\).

questions.prompt: Preview of poles and zeros. A system has \(G(j\omega)=100/(1+jf/10\ \mathrm{kHz})\). For an input of amplitude 1 at 100 kHz, what is the output amplitude?
questions.explanation:
At \(f=100\ \mathrm{kHz}\): \(f/f_{p}=10\), so \(|G|=100/\sqrt{1+100}=100/10.05=9.95\).
Output amplitude \(=1\times 9.95=9.95\).
The pole at 10 kHz has cut the gain from 100 to about 10 by 100 kHz (one decade above the pole: −20 dB). Common mistake: using the DC gain, giving 100.
